item.description:
Generic Warning | Yellow Warning - Rainfall - In Effect |

Heavy rain is expected over Central Saskatchewan, with total rainfall amounts of 40 to 60 mm. Rain will begin overnight in west central Saskatchewan and spread eastward through the day on Friday. Rain will continue through Sunday morning. In some locations, rain will be mixed with wet snow at times beginning early Saturday morning. Rain will change over to light snow late Saturday night, and then snow will gradually end Sunday morning. Water will likely pool on roads and in low-lying areas. Local utility outages are possible. Please continue to monitor alerts and forecasts issued by Environment Canada. item.title: Labour Mobility for Licensed Workers
item.description:
Labour Mobility for Licensed Workers jessicahughes Thu, 10/08/2026 - 09:51

PEI supports the movement of qualified workers across Canada through labour mobility provisions.

If you are certified in a regulated occupation in another Canadian province or territory, you may be eligible to have your credentials recognized in PEI without additional training, examinations, or work experience requirements.

The Canadian Free Trade Agreement (CFTA) supports labour mobility across Canada. Under Chapter 7 of the CFTA, workers certified by a regulator in one Canadian jurisdiction should generally be recognized by regulators in other jurisdictions.

Exceptions in PEI

PEI currently has approved exceptions for the following occupations:

  • Lawyer
  • Social Worker

Individuals in these occupations may need to demonstrate that they meet PEI-specific requirements before receiving certification.

For more information about labour mobility in Canada, please visit workersmobility.ca.

How do I Apply under Labour Mobility?

If you are certified in another Canadian province or territory:

Step 1

Find the regulatory body responsible for your profession in PEI.

Step 2

Submit a labour mobility application following the regulator's requirements. As part of the application process, regulators may request supporting information or documentation, including, but not limited to:

  • Proof of certification or licensure
  • Information on practice limitations, restrictions or conditions
  • Evidence of good character and professional standing
  • Demonstration of jurisdiction specific knowledge required for practice in PEI

Step 3

Once the regulator receives a complete application, a certification decision must be made within 30 calendar days.

Interprovincial Trade and Mobility Act (ITMA)

The Interprovincial Trade and Mobility Act and its regulations support faster labour mobility decisions for eligible professionals from reciprocal Canadian jurisdictions.

For eligible applications, regulatory bodies must make a decision within 10 days of receiving a complete application.

This streamlined process helps qualified professionals enter the PEI workforce more quickly.

Learn more: Interprovincial Trade and Mobility Act | Government of Prince Edward Island

item.title: Working in PEI with International Credentials
item.description:
Working in PEI with International Credentials jessicahughes Thu, 10/08/2026 - 09:36

If you completed your education or training outside Canada and want to work in a regulated occupation in Prince Edward Island, you will likely need to have your qualifications assessed before you can become licensed.

Foreign Credential Recognition (FCR) is the process used to determine whether education, skills, and work experience obtained outside Canada meet Canadian licensing requirements.

The credential recognition process varies depending on the occupation and the regulatory body responsible for licensing. The process may:

  • Require an assessment of your education, training, and work experience.
  • Include examinations, language proficiency testing, or additional training.
  • Involve application, assessment, and licensing fees.
  • Take several months or longer to complete, depending on the profession and individual circumstances.

Before you apply

Before applying for a license, you should:

  • Identify whether your occupation is regulated in PEI.
  • Contact the appropriate regulatory body to understand its licensing requirements.
  • Gather any required documents, such as transcripts, proof of identity, employment records, or professional certifications.

We encourage you to begin the credential recognition process before arriving in PEI whenever possible.

The Canadian Information Centre for International Credentials (CICIC) 

Learn more about the steps you may need to take to work in Canada.

item.title: Regulated Occupations
item.description:
Regulated Occupations jessicahughes Thu, 10/08/2026 - 09:24

Regulated occupations include professions and trades that are governed by legislation to protect public health, safety, and consumer interests.

To work in a regulated occupation in PEI, you must apply for certification or licensure through the appropriate regulatory body.

What Is a Regulatory Body?

A regulatory body (or regulator) is a government-approved organization responsible for governing a profession or trade.

Only individuals who meet the regulator's requirements can legally practice a regulated occupation in PEI.

item.title: Credential Recognition in PEI
item.description:
Credential Recognition in PEI jessicahughes Thu, 10/08/2026 - 08:50

This page provides information about regulated and non-regulated occupations, credential recognition, licensing requirements, and labour mobility options to help you work in your profession in PEI.

What is my occupation called in PEI?

Job titles and duties can vary between provinces and countries. Your occupation may have a different name in PEI, or the role may involve different responsibilities than you are accustomed to.

The Government of Canada's Job Bank can help you identify the PEI equivalent of your occupation and learn about:

  • Job duties and responsibilities
  • Employment demand in PEI
  • Current job opportunities
  • Employer locations across the provinces

Is my Occupation Regulated in PEI?

A regulated occupation is governed by provincial legislation and overseen by a regulatory body (also called a regulator or regulatory authority).

Regulatory bodies are responsible for:

  • Setting practice requirements 
  • Establishing professional standards
  • Assessing an applicant's qualifications and credentials
  • Issuing licenses, certifications, and registrations
  • Regulating professional conduct and discipline

These requirements help protect public health, safety, and consumer interests by ensuring professionals meet established standards.

If your occupation is regulated in PEI, you may need to obtain a license before you can legally work. Contact the appropriate regulatory body to determine the requirements for your profession. Regulators assess qualifications and credentials and may charge fees as part of the process.

How do I get Licensed in PEI?

Step 1: Find out if your occupation is regulated

Determine whether your profession or trade requires licensing or registration in PEI by consulting the regulated occupations directory.

Step 2: Contact the regulatory body

Visit the regulator's website and contact them directly.

Your regulatory body is the best source of information about:

  • Licensing or certification requirements
  • Application procedures
  • Required documentation
  • Processing timelines
  • Fees 

Step 3: Gather required documents

Requirements vary by occupation, but regulators commonly request:

  • Proof of identity
  • Educational credentials and certifications
  • Criminal record checks
  • Professional references
  • Proof of insurance or malpractice coverage

Step 4: Learn about application fees

Licensing and credential assessment fees vary by profession. Check the regulator's website or contact them directly to learn about costs associated with the licensure process.

Step 5: Complete an application form and submit required documents to your regulatory body

Complete the application form and submit all required documents and fees.

Regulators generally will not begin assessing an application until all required documents and fees have been received.

Looking for information specific to your situation?

  • Internationally trained workers – Learn about credential recognition if you completed your education or training outside of Canada.
  • Licensed in another Canadian province or territory – Learn how labour mobility provisions may apply if you already hold a license elsewhere in Canada.

What if my Occupation is not Regulated?

Most occupations in PEI are non-regulated, meaning a license or certification is not required to work. While credential assessments are generally not required for non-regulated occupations, they can help employers understand how international education and training compare to Canadian standards.

Employers typically want to know that candidates have the education, skills, and work experience needed to perform the job. If you completed your education or training outside Canada, you may wish to ask prospective employers whether they would like to see a credential assessment or evaluation of your work experience.

Need Help?

If you have questions about credential recognition, licensing requirements, or the registration process, we are here to help.

Labour Mobility and Foreign Credential Recognition Coordinator

briannaesquires@gov.pe.ca

We can help you understand your options, connect with the appropriate regulator, and provide information on the credential recognition process.

item.title: Province adds 82 new long-term care beds at Whisperwood
item.description:
Province adds 82 new long-term care beds at Whisperwood jenniferdhogan Tue, 10/06/2026 - 15:31

The Government of Prince Edward Island announced today that 82 new long-term care beds will be added at Whisperwood nursing home in Charlottetown, helping more Island seniors access quality care close to home.

Enhanced Living has been awarded the contract to expand its Whisperwood facility and operate the new beds. The project will increase long-term care capacity in Queens County and help meet growing demand as Prince Edward Island’s population continues to grow and age. 

The province will provide $3.5 million annually over a 30-year agreement to support construction costs. Once the new beds are operational, the province will provide an estimated $10.1 million annually to help offset accommodation costs for the residents.

Today’s announcement marks a significant step in the province’s efforts to strengthen long-term care and improve healthcare capacity across Prince Edward Island. 

With the addition of the Whisperwood expansion, 222 new long-term care beds are now under development in Charlottetown, Cornwall and Summerside. The province has also issued a Request for Proposals through the Provincial Long-Term Care Program for up to 48 new long-term care beds in Kings County. 

Increasing long-term care capacity is a key part of the province’s plan to improve care for seniors, support Islanders to remain safely in their homes longer, and ensure hospital beds are available for patients who need acute care services. 

Long-term care services in Prince Edward Island are delivered through nine public and 11 private long-term care homes, as well as 36 community care facilities. With the projects currently underway, the total number of long-term care beds in the province is expected to increase to 1,595 by 2029.

For more information, visit Long-term Care | Government of Prince Edward Island.

Quotes:

“Island seniors deserve access to quality care when they need it, and families deserve the peace of mind that comes with knowing their loved ones are well supported. This expansion at Whisperwood will create 82 new long-term care spaces, strengthen healthcare capacity, and help ensure more Islanders can access the care they need close to home. It's another example of the investments we're making to build a stronger healthcare system for Islanders today and for the future.”

- Premier Rob Lantz

“As seniors’ needs change, the right level of care should be there for them. These 82 new beds will help more Islanders access long-term care while staying close to family and the places they know best. We’re proud to partner with Enhanced Living on this project and build on the excellent care already being provided at Whisperwood.”

- Minister of Health and Wellness Cory Deagle

“Whisperwood has been part of our community for many years, and many Charlottetown families know it well. This expansion means more seniors will be able to stay close to their loved ones while getting the high-quality care and support they need.”

- Charlottetown-Belvedere MLA Susie Dillon

“This expansion at Whisperwood is an important investment for our community and the people who call Charlottetown home. As Charlottetown continues to grow, so does the need for health care services that support residents at every stage of life. The addition of 82 long-term care beds will help meet the changing needs of our community and provide more options for seniors and their families.”

- City of Charlottetown Mayor Philip Brown 

"We're delighted to partner with the province on this expansion of Whisperwood, a home our community knows and trusts. This expansion will allow us to welcome additional residents and provide them with the very best care, while helping to free up critical hospital beds for Islanders who need acute care.”

- Enhanced Living Chief Financial Officer Joshua Simon

item.title: Premier McLeod on the Enbridge Line 21 Pipeline
item.description:
YELLOWKNIFE - Premier Bob McLeod issued the following statement on the Enbridge Line 21 pipeline today:

“I was pleased to learn that operations have resumed for Enbridge’s Line 21 pipeline after almost 2 years of no activity.

"Resource development has, and will continue to be, the backbone of our economy and is central to ensuring a good source of middle class jobs and business opportunities. Our territory has mineral and petroleum resources and the development of those resources can have a transformative effect on our people and economy.

"Sustainable economic development is key to the future of Northerners. With a strong resource development base, we will be able to support diversification of our local economies into emerging and established sectors.

"On behalf of the Government of the Northwest Territories I’d like to offer my congratulations to Imperial Oil, Enbridge the town of Norman Wells and other partners for getting this pipeline back up and running. I know the efforts and economic impacts of the pipeline have already begun to take shape in the community and will be felt for years to come. ”
